orig_9709_s1_bg_binomial_models.description: Justify a binomial model and translate exact counts, tails and intervals into probabilities.

sections.title: A count model and its lower tail
sections.label: Count an exact number of successes
sections.intro: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.

blocks.html:
A fixed number of trials and a fixed definition of success

For a binomial model, count successes in a fixed number n of independent trials. Each trial must have the same success probability p and only success or failure relative to the chosen definition. A trial may have several physical outcomes, provided they are grouped consistently into these two categories.

\[X\sim\mathrm B(n,p).\]

blocks.title: Count an exact number of successes
blocks.prompt: \(X\) counts successes in five independent trials with success probability \(\frac13\). Find \(\mathrm P(X=2)\).
blocks.hint: Choose two success positions. Each pattern has two success factors and three failure factors.
blocks.solution:
Choose two success positions. Each pattern has two success factors and three failure factors.

  • Answer: \(\frac{80}{243}\)

sections.title: Define success before using moments
sections.label: Use binomial moments

blocks.html:
One count can be reached in several orders

For exactly r successes, one specified order has probability \(p^r(1-p)^{n-r}\). Choose the r successful positions to account for all orders.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\binom nr p^r(1-p)^{n-r}.\]

The support is the integers from 0 to n. The combination factor is not needed for a single specified order, such as failure on every trial except the last.

blocks.title: Use binomial moments
blocks.prompt: Find the variance of \(X\sim\mathrm B(8,\frac14)\).
blocks.hint: Use \(np(1-p)\) with the success and failure probabilities kept separate.
blocks.solution:
Use \(np(1-p)\) with the success and failure probabilities kept separate.

  • Answer: \(\frac{3}{2}\)

sections.title: Strict endpoints select integer values
sections.label: Translate a strict count

blocks.html:
Translate the endpoint words first

At most k means \(X\le k\); fewer than k means \(X\le k-1\). At least k means \(X\ge k\); more than k means \(X\ge k+1\). A strict interval \(L<X<U\) includes only the integers \(L+1\) through \(U-1\).

\[\mathrm P(X\ge k)=1-\mathrm P(X\le k-1).\]

For at least one success, subtract the probability of no successes. For a small central interval, add its point probabilities. Do not use a complement with the wrong endpoint.

blocks.title: Translate a strict count
blocks.prompt: For six trials, give the smallest count included by the event “more than three successes”.
blocks.hint: Counts are integers. The strict comparison excludes three.
blocks.solution:
Counts are integers. The strict comparison excludes three.

  • Answer: \(4\)

sections.title: A specified order differs from an unspecified count
sections.label: Read a specified order

blocks.html:
State the assumptions in context

Sampling a changing finite population without replacement is not exactly binomial. A common batch quality can also make outcomes dependent. Independence is a model assumption that needs a reason, not a consequence of observing repeated trials.

blocks.title: Read a specified order
blocks.prompt: For three independent trials with success probability \(\frac14\), find the probability of success, failure, success in that order.
blocks.hint: This event specifies one pattern. Multiply its three probabilities directly.
blocks.solution:
This event specifies one pattern. Multiply its three probabilities directly.

  • Answer: \(\frac{3}{64}\)

blocks.html:
• Include the combination factor for an unspecified set of success positions.
  • At least k is complemented by at most k−1.
  • Do not interchange successes and failures without changing p.
  • A fixed number of trials differs from stopping on first success.

examples.title: A count model and its lower tail
examples.question: A sensor is tested 4 times independently. Each test fails with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). X counts failed tests. Give n and p in its binomial model, then \(\mathrm P(X=1)\) and \(\mathrm P(X\le 2)\).
solution: Failure is the defined success for this count. The trials are fixed, independent and share a constant probability.

examples.title: Define success before using moments
examples.question: On each independent run a device gives red with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), amber with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), and green otherwise. X counts red-or-amber results in 5 runs. Find its success probability, mean, variance and \(\mathrm P(X\ge 1)\).
solution: Red and amber are disjoint categories of the same run, so add their probabilities. Then use the binomial moments and complement the zero-count event.

examples.title: Strict endpoints select integer values
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(5,\frac{2}{5})\). Find \(\mathrm P(1<X<4)\), \(\mathrm P(X\ge 4)\), and \(\mathrm P(X=3 \mid 1<X<4)\).
solution: The strict interval retains integer counts 2, 3. Add those entries. The upper event includes its endpoint. In the conditional event, the requested point is already within the interval.

examples.title: A specified order differs from an unspecified count
examples.question: There are 5 independent trials, each with success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the probability of exactly one success anywhere, of the last trial being the only success, and of at least one success. Choose the correct explanation.
solution: There are n possible positions for an unspecified single success. The specified last-success history is one sequence only. At least one is the complement of all failures.
Correct conclusion: An unspecified single success can occupy n positions; the specified last success cannot.

glossary.definition: One repetition of the same experiment.
The outcome the model counts.
The number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.
The number of trials up to and including the first success.

revision.checks:
1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.
revision.examTip: Include the combination factor for an unspecified set of success positions.

orig_9709_s1_bg_inverse_binomial.description: Recover binomial parameters and find exact integer bounds while retaining all feasible branches.

sections.title: Recover trial count and success probability
sections.label: Recover both binomial parameters
sections.intro: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.

blocks.html:
The mean and variance identify different quantities

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm E(X)&=np,\\\operatorname{Var}(X)&=np(1-p).\end{aligned}\]

If a standard deviation is supplied, square it before using the variance equation. The mean is measured in counts and the variance in squared counts. For a non-degenerate model with positive mean, divide the variance by the mean to find \(1-p\), then recover n. Check \(0<p<1\) and that n is a positive integer.

\[p=1-\frac{v}{\mu},\qquad n=\frac{\mu}{p}.\]

blocks.title: Recover both binomial parameters
blocks.prompt: A binomial variable has mean \(9\) and variance \(6\). Find its trial count and success probability.
blocks.hint: Dividing variance by mean gives \(1-p=\frac23\). Then use \(np=9\).
blocks.solution:
Dividing variance by mean gives \(1-p=\frac23\). Then use \(np=9\).

  • Trial count: \(27\)
  • Success probability: \(\frac{1}{3}\)

sections.title: A known mean supplies p
sections.label: Keep both permitted probabilities

blocks.html:
Check the original model after solving

A numerical solution with n not an integer is not a binomial trial count. A negative variance, or variance greater than the mean in a non-degenerate binomial model, signals an invalid parameter set. The deterministic boundary cases \(p=0\) and \(p=1\) need separate interpretation.

blocks.title: Keep both permitted probabilities
blocks.prompt: A binomial variable has trial count \(16\) and variance \(3\). Give both possible success probabilities.
blocks.hint: The quadratic is \(p(1-p)=\frac{3}{16}\). Both roots lie strictly between zero and one.
blocks.solution:
The quadratic is \(p(1-p)=\frac{3}{16}\). Both roots lie strictly between zero and one.

  • Answer: \(\left\{\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}\right\}\)

sections.title: Inclusive and strict targets can differ by one trial
sections.label: Include a boundary that qualifies

blocks.html:
A probability target gives a bound, not an automatic integer

For at least one success in n trials the probability is \(1-(1-p)^n\). This increases with n. A logarithmic estimate can locate the boundary, but the original strict or inclusive inequality decides which integer is valid.

Check the neighbouring trial counts

For a minimum, verify that the proposed integer satisfies the condition and the preceding integer does not. If the target equals a boundary probability, changing ≥ to > can increase the minimum by one. For a maximum survival condition, check the next integer instead. Do not round a logarithm to the nearest integer without checking.

blocks.title: Include a boundary that qualifies
blocks.prompt: Each independent trial succeeds with probability \(\frac12\). Find the least trial count for which the chance of at least one success is at least \(\frac78\).
blocks.hint: The failure run must have probability at most \(\frac18\). Three trials meet equality.
blocks.solution:
The failure run must have probability at most \(\frac18\). Three trials meet equality.

  • Answer: \(3\)

sections.title: Variance can determine two branches
sections.label: Check a strict target

blocks.html:
Variance alone can leave two values of p

For known n, \(p(1-p)\) is unchanged when p is replaced by \(1-p\). Solve the quadratic, retain both valid values, and use any extra mean or context restriction only afterwards. Label the smaller and larger answers clearly.

blocks.title: Check a strict target
blocks.prompt: Use independent trials with success probability \(\frac12\). Find the least trial count making the chance of at least one success strictly more than \(\frac78\).
blocks.hint: Three trials give equality. Four trials make the failure run strictly less than \(\frac18\).
blocks.solution:
Three trials give equality. Four trials make the failure run strictly less than \(\frac18\).

  • Answer: \(4\)

blocks.html:
• Square a given standard deviation before substituting for variance.
  • Do not discard p and \(1-p\) without an extra restriction.
  • n must be an integer, not a rounded estimate that changes the given model.
  • Strict and inclusive probability targets can have different integer answers.

examples.title: Recover trial count and success probability
examples.question: X is binomial with mean \(\frac{4}{3}\) and variance \(\frac{8}{9}\). Find n, p and \(\mathrm P(X=2)\).
solution: Divide the variance equation by the mean equation, then recover the trial count. Verify p lies in (0,1) and n is an integer.

examples.title: A known mean supplies p
examples.question: X is binomial with 3 trials and mean \(1\). Find p, \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\), and \(\mathrm P(X=1 \mid X\le 2)\).
solution: Use \(np\) equal to the given mean. The conditional point is allowed by the upper bound, so divide its probability by the inclusive lower tail.

examples.title: Inclusive and strict targets can differ by one trial
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the minimum n for the probability of at least one success in n trials to be at least \(\frac{37}{64}\), and separately to be greater than this target. Give the at-least-one probability at the inclusive minimum.
solution: The relevant cumulative probability is \(1-(1-p)^n\). Check the original inequality at consecutive integers; equality is allowed only for the inclusive target.

examples.title: Variance can determine two branches
examples.question: X is binomial with 6 trials and variance \(\frac{5}{6}\). Find both possible success probabilities, labelled smaller and larger, and the corresponding means in the same order.
solution: Rearrange \(np(1-p)\) equal to the given variance as a quadratic. Its valid roots are complementary. No extra information here selects one branch.

orig_9709_s1_bg_mixed_binomial.description: Combine groups and batches correctly, retain shared causes and condition on the actual count event.

sections.title: One success overall has two disjoint routes
sections.label: Add the routes for one success
sections.intro: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.

blocks.html:
Groups with different probabilities need separate counts

If two independent groups have different success probabilities, their combined count is not generally binomial with an averaged p. To get one success overall, split into one from the first group and none from the second, or the reverse. Add disjoint cases and retain their labels for a posterior question.

blocks.title: Add the routes for one success
blocks.prompt: Two independent attempts have success probabilities \(\frac13\) and \(\frac14\). Find the probability of exactly one success.
blocks.hint: Add the two orders in which exactly one attempt succeeds.
blocks.solution:
Add the two orders in which exactly one attempt succeeds.

  • Answer: \(\frac{5}{12}\)

sections.title: A common machine makes the trials dependent
sections.label: Condition on the shared machine

blocks.html:
A shared hidden choice can create dependence

A machine chosen once for a batch affects every item in that batch. Trials may be independent conditional on the machine, yet dependent after its identity is hidden. Mix the full conditional count tables using the machine-choice weights. The binomial variance formula using an averaged p need not apply to that mixture.

blocks.title: Condition on the shared machine
blocks.prompt: Choose A or B with equal probability, then use that machine for both trials. The trials are independent given the machine, with success probability \(\frac12\) on A and \(\frac14\) on B. Find the probability both trials succeed.
blocks.hint: Square each machine's success probability before averaging the two results.
blocks.solution:
Square each machine's success probability before averaging the two results.

  • Answer: \(\frac{5}{32}\)

sections.title: Qualifying batches form the outer count
sections.label: Choose the batch success event

blocks.html:
A batch event can become a new Bernoulli success

First calculate q, the probability a batch meets its stated criterion. If batches are independent and identically generated, the number of qualifying batches in a fixed set is binomial with success probability q. It is q, not the probability of a single item, that belongs in the second model.

blocks.title: Choose the batch success event
blocks.prompt: Two independent devices each fail with probability \(\frac14\). A batch fails when either device fails. Find the batch failure probability.
blocks.hint: Use the complement of both devices passing.
blocks.solution:
Use the complement of both devices passing.

  • Answer: \(\frac{7}{16}\)

sections.title: Condition on at least one success
sections.label: Condition on a nonzero count

blocks.html:
Restrict and renormalise a count table

Let H be a count event with positive probability. Intersect the requested event with H and divide by \(\mathrm P(H)\). For conditional moments, retain only the permitted count values and renormalise their probabilities.

\[\mathrm P(X=r\mid H)=\frac{\mathrm P(\{X=r\}\cap H)}{\mathrm P(H)}.\]

Given at least one success, the zero-count outcome is removed. The conditional mean is not simply \(np\). Keep the condition explicit in both probability and expectation notation.

blocks.title: Condition on a nonzero count
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm B(2,\frac14)\). Find \(\mathrm P(X=2\mid X>0)\).
blocks.hint: Divide the probability of two successes by the probability of at least one.
blocks.solution:
Divide the probability of two successes by the probability of at least one.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{7}\)

blocks.html:
• Averaging different group probabilities does not generally give the combined model.
  • Use the batch qualification probability in the outer binomial.
  • Conditional independence does not force unconditional independence.
  • Conditional expectations need a normalised conditional distribution.

examples.title: One success overall has two disjoint routes
examples.question: Group A has 2 trials with success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\); group B has 3 trials with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). All trials are independent. Find the probabilities of no successes overall, exactly one overall, and that the unique success came from A given exactly one overall.
solution: For one overall, use the disjoint cases (one in A, none in B) and (none in A, one in B). Keep the first case as the posterior numerator.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(A_1\cap B_0)&=\frac{3}{64},\\{}\mathrm P(A_0\cap B_1)&=\frac{27}{128},\\{}\mathrm P(\text{one overall})&=\frac{33}{128},\\{}\mathrm P(A_1\mid\text{one overall})&=\frac{\frac{3}{64}}{\frac{33}{128}}.\end{aligned}\]
Unique success from A given exactly one: \(\frac{2}{11}\).

examples.title: A common machine makes the trials dependent
examples.question: Choose machine A once with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), otherwise B. Test two items using that same machine. Conditional on its identity, outcomes are independent with success probability \(\frac{1}{5}\) for A or \(\frac{3}{5}\) for B. X counts the two successes. Find the marginal success probability of one item, \(\mathrm P(X=2)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\), then choose the dependence statement.
solution: Weight the two conditional binomial tables by the initial machine-choice probabilities. Calculate the variance from this mixture. Compare the joint success probability with the square of the marginal probability.
Correct conclusion: The shared hidden machine makes the outcomes dependent unconditionally.

examples.title: Qualifying batches form the outer count
examples.question: A batch contains 3 independent items, each successful with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). It qualifies if at least 2 succeed. There are 2 independent such batches; K counts qualifying batches. Find the qualification probability q, \(\mathrm E(K)\), and \(\mathrm P(K=1)\).
solution: First evaluate the inner binomial upper tail. Each batch then supplies one independent success/failure indicator with probability q; use that in the outer binomial.

examples.title: Condition on at least one success
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(3,\frac{1}{3})\). Let \(H=\{X\ge1\}\). Find \(\mathrm P(X=2 \mid H)\), \(\mathrm P(X\le 2 \mid H)\), and \(\mathrm E(X \mid H)\).
solution: Remove the zero-count outcome and divide every retained probability by \(\mathrm P(H)\). Both the lower tail and the mean use the renormalised table.

Complete answers

Point probability given at least one: \(\frac{6}{19}\).

orig_9709_s1_bg_geometric.description: Use the first-success convention, waiting-time tails, memorylessness and finite caps correctly.

sections.title: A point, a tail and a cumulative probability
sections.label: Count the earlier failures
sections.intro: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.

blocks.html:
Count trials including the first success

Repeat independent trials with a constant success probability p until the first success. For \(0<p\le1\), the trial count T has support \(1,2,3,\ldots\) and is written \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\). It counts the successful trial as well as the preceding failures.

\[\begin{aligned}T&\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p),\\\mathrm P(T=r)&=(1-p)^{r-1}p.\end{aligned}\]

blocks.title: Count the earlier failures
blocks.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac14\). Find the probability the first success occurs on trial three.
blocks.hint: Two failures precede the success on the third trial.
blocks.solution:
Two failures precede the success on the third trial.

  • Answer: \(\frac{9}{64}\)

sections.title: The further wait restarts, but the total clock does not
sections.label: Translate the waiting tail

blocks.html:
Tail events describe runs of failures

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(T>m)&=(1-p)^m,\\\mathrm P(T\le m)&=1-(1-p)^m.\end{aligned}\]

\(T>m\) means all first m trials failed. \(T\ge m\) needs only the first \(m-1\) failures. For an interval, subtract the relevant tails with these exact endpoints.

The expected wait and a restart

\[\mathrm E(T)=\frac1p.\]

After a known run of failures, the further wait still has the same geometric law, because the remaining independent trials are unchanged. The expected number of further trials is \(\frac1p\); the expected total trial count includes the failures already observed. State which of these the question asks for.

blocks.title: Translate the waiting tail
blocks.prompt: For a geometric waiting time \(T\) with success probability \(\frac12\), find \(\mathrm P(T>4)\).
blocks.hint: The first four trials must all fail.
blocks.solution:
The first four trials must all fail.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{16}\)

sections.title: A consecutive-probability ratio gives the failure probability
sections.label: Recover the trial probability

blocks.html:
Recover p from the correct information

The ratio of consecutive positive point probabilities is \(1-p\). The reciprocal of a given mean is p. In either case check the probability range and use neighbouring integers for a strict or inclusive waiting-time target.

blocks.title: Recover the trial probability
blocks.prompt: For a geometric waiting time \(T\), the ratio \(\frac{\mathrm P(T=3)}{\mathrm P(T=2)}\) is \(\frac23\). Find the trial success probability.
blocks.hint: The extra failure factor is \(1-p=\frac23\).
blocks.solution:
The extra failure factor is \(1-p=\frac23\).

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{3}\)

sections.title: The last capped value combines success and failure
sections.label: Combine both routes into the cap

blocks.html:
A capped wait is a different variable

If \(N=\min(T,c)\), then \(N=c\) includes success on c and failure on every one of the c trials. Hence \(\mathrm P(N=c)\) is the probability of reaching trial c, not just of succeeding on it. Build the finite table and calculate \(\mathrm E(N)\) from it; the unrestricted formula \(\frac1p\) is not \(\mathrm E(N)\).

blocks.title: Combine both routes into the cap
blocks.prompt: Let \(W=\min(T,4)\), where \(T\) is the first success with probability \(\frac14\) per independent trial. Find \(\mathrm P(W=4)\).
blocks.hint: Every wait of at least four contributes to the cap. Only the first three failures are required.
blocks.solution:
Every wait of at least four contributes to the cap. Only the first three failures are required.

  • Answer: \(\frac{27}{64}\)

blocks.html:
• \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) starts at 1, not 0.
  • \(T\ge m\) and \(T>m\) have different failure counts.
  • Expected further trials and expected total trials are different after known failures.
  • At a finite cap combine terminal success and failure outcomes.

examples.title: A point, a tail and a cumulative probability
examples.question: Independent trials have constant success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). T is the first-success trial, including the successful trial. Find \(\mathrm P(T=3)\), \(\mathrm P(T>4)\), \(\mathrm P(T\le 4)\), and \(\mathrm E(T)\).
solution: The point event needs 2 failures followed by success. The tail needs all first 4 trials to fail. The cumulative probability is its complement.

Complete answers

First success on the stated trial: \(\frac{18}{125}\).

examples.title: The further wait restarts, but the total clock does not
examples.question: T is geometric with success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). The first 2 trials have failed. Find \(\mathrm P(T>4 \mid T>2)\), \(\mathrm P(T=4 \mid T>2)\), the expected number of further trials, and the expected total trial count.
solution: Cancel the already observed failure factor from numerator and denominator. The remaining future trials keep the original success probability. The total clock adds the known failures to the further wait.

Complete answers

Conditional probability of the later tail: \(\frac{9}{25}\).

examples.title: A consecutive-probability ratio gives the failure probability
examples.question: T is the first-success trial count in independent trials with constant success probability p. The ratio \(\mathrm P(T=3)\)/\(\mathrm P(T=2)\) is \(\frac{3}{4}\). Find p, \(\mathrm E(T)\), the minimum n with \(\mathrm P(T\le n)\) at least \(\frac{37}{64}\), and the minimum n when the inequality is strict.
solution: The consecutive point-probability ratio is \(1-p\), so subtract it from one; the mean is \(\frac1p\).
The relevant cumulative probability is \(1-(1-p)^n\). Check the original inequality at consecutive integers; equality is allowed only for the inclusive target.

examples.title: The last capped value combines success and failure
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). T is the unrestricted first-success trial. Stop after at most 4 attempts and let \(N=\min(T,4)\). Find \(\mathrm P(N=4)\), \(\mathrm E(N)\), the probability of success by the cap, and \(\mathrm E(T)\).
solution: The last value combines success on trial c and no success in the allowed trials. Their sum is the chance of reaching trial c. Use the finite table for N; \(\frac1p\) belongs to the unrestricted T.

Complete answers

Probability at the capped final value: \(\frac{27}{64}\).

related.title: Repeated successes and mixed stopping rules

glossary.definition: One repetition of the same experiment.
The outcome the model counts.
The number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.
The number of trials up to and including the first success.

revision.body:
Count trials including the first success

Repeat independent trials with a constant success probability p until the first success. For \(0<p\le1\), the trial count T has support \(1,2,3,\ldots\) and is written \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\). It counts the successful trial as well as the preceding failures.

\[\begin{aligned}T&\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p),\\\mathrm P(T=r)&=(1-p)^{r-1}p.\end{aligned}\]

Tail events describe runs of failures

\(T>m\) means all first m trials failed. \(T\ge m\) needs only the first \(m-1\) failures. For an interval, subtract the relevant tails with these exact endpoints.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(T>m)&=(1-p)^m,\\\mathrm P(T\le m)&=1-(1-p)^m.\end{aligned}\]

The expected wait and a restart

After a known run of failures, the further wait still has the same geometric law, because the remaining independent trials are unchanged. The expected number of further trials is \(\frac1p\); the expected total trial count includes the failures already observed. State which of these the question asks for.

\[\mathrm E(T)=\frac1p.\]

Recover p from the correct information

The ratio of consecutive positive point probabilities is \(1-p\). The reciprocal of a given mean is p. In either case check the probability range and use neighbouring integers for a strict or inclusive waiting-time target.

A capped wait is a different variable

If \(N=\min(T,c)\), then \(N=c\) includes success on c and failure on every one of the c trials. Hence \(\mathrm P(N=c)\) is the probability of reaching trial c, not just of succeeding on it. Build the finite table and calculate \(\mathrm E(N)\) from it; the unrestricted formula \(\frac1p\) is not \(\mathrm E(N)\).

1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.

orig_9709_s1_bg_success_sequences.description: Count success positions and terminal histories without applying an unrequired named distribution.

sections.title: Fix the final trial of the second success
sections.label: Fix the last success
sections.intro: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.

blocks.html:
A second success fixes the final trial

For the second success on trial t, the first t−1 trials contain exactly one success and trial t succeeds. Use the earlier binomial count and multiply by the final success probability. This is a construction from familiar methods; no negative-binomial theorem is required.

\[\mathrm P(S_2=t)=\mathrm P(\mathrm B(t-1,p)=1)\,p.\]

By a trial and on a trial are different events

The second success by trial m is equivalent to at least two successes in the first m trials. The second success exactly on m excludes histories that had already reached two successes earlier. A specified first-success position can impose further restrictions on those earlier histories.

blocks.title: Fix the last success
blocks.prompt: Each independent trial succeeds with probability \(\frac12\). Find the probability the second success occurs at trial five.
blocks.hint: There must be one success among the first four trials and a success at trial five.
blocks.solution:
There must be one success among the first four trials and a success at trial five.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{8}\)

sections.title: Two waiting clocks can finish together
sections.label: Keep the two waiting times separate

blocks.html:
Independent waiting processes keep separate parameters

For two independent first-success processes, multiply their point probabilities for a specified pair of finish times. Sum disjoint pairs for events such as simultaneous finishes within a finite window. Given both finish in that window, divide by the probability of that condition.

blocks.title: Keep the two waiting times separate
blocks.prompt: Two independent sequences both succeed with probability \(\frac12\) per trial. Find the probability their first successes both occur at trial two.
blocks.hint: Each sequence must fail and then succeed. Multiply the two sequence probabilities.
blocks.solution:
Each sequence must fail and then succeed. Multiply the two sequence probabilities.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{16}\)

sections.title: A finite bag is not an independent-trial model
sections.label: Find a marked position

blocks.html:
Sampling without replacement changes the hazard

A first marked item in a finite bag has a changing success chance after each failure. Use the finite tree or marked-position subsets. The initial success proportion alone does not justify \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) or the mean \(\frac1p\).

blocks.title: Find a marked position
blocks.prompt: Shuffle four white counters and one red counter. Find the probability the red counter first appears on draw three.
blocks.hint: Each of the five positions is equally likely for the unique red counter.
blocks.solution:
Each of the five positions is equally likely for the unique red counter.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{5}\)

sections.title: Stop on either of two competing targets
sections.label: Stop on either event

blocks.html:
Stop immediately when either condition is met

In a race to two successes or two failures, SS and FF end after two trials. Only SF and FS continue. On trial three every remaining path ends. List these terminal histories once, multiply their probabilities and check that the total is one. Never append a trial to an already stopped history.

blocks.title: Stop on either event
blocks.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac35\). Stop after two successes or after the first failure. Find the probability the stopping time is exactly two.
blocks.hint: The first trial must succeed. Either outcome of the second trial stops the experiment.
blocks.solution:
The first trial must succeed. Either outcome of the second trial stops the experiment.

  • Answer: \(\frac{3}{5}\)

blocks.html:
• The final success needs its own probability factor.
  • Second success on t excludes an earlier second success.
  • A first success in a finite bag need not be geometric.
  • Do not count histories after a stopping condition has already occurred.

examples.title: Fix the final trial of the second success
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Let S₂ be the trial of the second success. Find \(\mathrm P(S₂=4)\), \(\mathrm P(S₂\le 5)\), and the probability the first success is on trial 1 and the second on trial 4.
solution: For the second success on t, use exactly one success among the first t−1 trials and success on trial t. For the joint event, the first and final trials succeed and every intervening trial fails.

Complete answers

Second success on the stated trial: \(\frac{108}{625}\).
First on one and second on the stated trial: \(\frac{36}{625}\).

examples.title: Two waiting clocks can finish together
examples.question: Two independent processes have first-success trial counts T_A and T_B, with success probabilities \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the probability both finish by 3, exactly one finishes by 3, and that they finish on the same trial given both finish by 3.
solution: For both, multiply the two cumulative probabilities. Exactly one has two disjoint routes. For simultaneous finishes within the window, sum products of matching point probabilities, then condition on both finishing.
Same finish time given both finish by the limit: \(\frac{97}{259}\).

examples.title: A finite bag is not an independent-trial model
examples.question: A bag contains 2 marked and 4 unmarked counters. Draw uniformly without replacement until the first marked counter appears; T is its position. Find \(\mathrm P(T=3)\), \(\mathrm E(T)\), and choose the correct model statement.
solution: In a random order every subset of marked positions is equally likely. For \(T=t\), the first marked position is t and the other marked positions are chosen afterwards. The finite table sums to one; it does not have a geometric tail.

Complete answers

Probability of first marked on trial three: \(\frac{1}{5}\).
Correct conclusion: The success probability changes after failure; use a finite model.

examples.title: Stop on either of two competing targets
examples.question: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Stop as soon as two successes or two failures have occurred. T is the number of trials and W means stopping with two successes. Find \(\mathrm P(W)\), \(\mathrm P(T=3)\), \(\mathrm E(T)\), and \(\mathrm P(W \mid T=3)\).
solution: SS and FF stop immediately. SF and FS each allow one more trial. These six terminal histories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; no trial follows an already stopped path.

Complete answers

Probability of stopping with two successes: \(\frac{5}{32}\).
